summary: Describes EtherIP, an early and very lightweight tunneling protocol that carries Ethernet and IEEE 802.3 frames inside IP datagrams so non-IP traffic can cross an IP network. It is written for historical context for IP protocol number 97, and it does not protect against infinite loops.

eli5.summary: EtherIP puts a whole local-network message inside an ordinary internet package, like a letter inside a bigger envelope, so it can travel across the internet.

questions: how to tunnel ethernet over ip
subtitle: Tunneling Ethernet frames inside IP datagrams for non-IP traffic

tldr.problem: Some networks or applications use protocols other than IP over Ethernet, or encrypt their payloads, making IP routing impossible. Ethernet segments may be geographically separated and need to communicate across an IP internet.
tldr.mechanism: EtherIP encapsulates entire Ethernet or IEEE 802.3 frames (minus the frame check sequence) in a simple 16-bit header, then wraps them in IP datagrams to send them across an IP network to a remote EtherIP station.
tldr.outcome: EtherIP enables communication between distant Ethernet segments but is very lightweight and offers no protection against routing loops. Better protocols have since been developed.

today: EtherIP remains documented for historical and informational purposes. The protocol is rarely used in new deployments. Modern standards like L2TP and Pseudo Wire Emulation (PWE3) provide more robust Ethernet tunneling with better loop detection, quality of service, and security properties. IPsec can be used to protect EtherIP datagrams when carrying sensitive encrypted traffic.

sections.title: Introduction and History
sections.content:
The EtherIP protocol was first designed and developed in 1991 as a simple way to tunnel Ethernet and IEEE 802.3 frames across an IP internet. This RFC documents the protocol for historical and informational purposes to explain the assignment of IP protocol 97.

EtherIP is one of the earliest tunneling protocols. It is very lightweight, containing only a 16-bit header, but it provides no protection against infinite routing loops. More recent IETF standards for tunneling Ethernet frames—such as those produced by the Layer Two Tunneling Protocol Extensions (L2TPEXT) and Pseudo Wire Emulation Edge-to-Edge (PWE3) working groups—overcome the deficiencies of EtherIP and should be used instead for new deployments.
sections.eli5: EtherIP was invented in 1991 as a simple way to wrap Ethernet messages in internet packages. There are better ways to do this now, but this document explains how EtherIP works.

sections.title: When EtherIP Is Used
sections.content:
EtherIP tunnels are useful when the layer three protocol carried in Ethernet frames is not IP, or when the payload is encrypted. For example, two Ethernet stations using the Xerox Network Systems Internetwork Datagram Protocol (IDP) at different physical locations could use EtherIP to communicate across the Internet. Another example is Ethernet stations using IEEE 802.10b secure data exchange that encrypt their payloads; EtherIP allows them to tunnel their encrypted Ethernet frames across an IP internet without the IP network needing to decrypt and understand the contents.

EtherIP can be implemented in an end station to enable tunneling for that single station based on criteria such as destination address or EtherType. Alternatively, it can be implemented in a bridge-like station to provide tunneling services for all stations connected to a particular Ethernet segment. The bridge listens to all traffic on the segment, examines frames to determine which need tunneling, and forwards them to a remote bridge-like station via IP.
sections.eli5: EtherIP is useful if you have computers on separate Ethernet networks that speak a language other than IP, or that encrypt their messages, and you want to let them talk across the internet.

sections.title: Protocol Format
sections.content:
An EtherIP datagram consists of an IP header, a 16-bit EtherIP header, and an encapsulated Ethernet or IEEE 802.3 frame (without the frame check sequence). The 16-bit EtherIP header has two parts: a 4-bit version field and a 12-bit reserved field for future use. The version field MUST be set to 3 (three, binary '0011'). The reserved field MUST be set to zero. Earlier versions of the protocol used an 8-bit header; the 16-bit header was introduced to provide memory alignment advantages in some implementation environments.

The IPv4 Protocol field MUST be set to 97 (decimal) to identify the datagram as EtherIP. The encapsulated Ethernet frame field contains a complete Ethernet or IEEE 802.3 frame of any type less the frame check sequence (FCS) value. The IP checksum does not provide integrity protection for the tunneled Ethernet frame, so higher-layer protocols encapsulated within the Ethernet frame are expected to provide integrity protection if needed.
sections.eli5: The header is tiny—just 16 bits—and it tells the receiver 'this is EtherIP version 3 and I have an Ethernet frame inside.' The frame itself is just a regular Ethernet message with its error-check removed.

sections.title: Sending and Receiving
sections.content:
When a sender wants to transmit an Ethernet frame via EtherIP, it first determines whether tunneling is needed. If the recipient is on the same local network or if the network can already route the protocol, tunneling is not needed. Otherwise, the sender prepends the 16-bit EtherIP header (with version 3 and reserved field zero), determines the destination IP address of the remote EtherIP station (usually from the destination MAC address), and wraps the result in an IP datagram with Protocol field 97. The datagram is then transmitted to the remote EtherIP station via the local IP router.

At the receiving end, a station processes incoming datagrams by checking that the IPv4 Protocol field is 97 (decimal) and examining the EtherIP header to confirm the version is 3 and the reserved field is zero. Invalid frames are discarded. The encapsulated Ethernet frame is extracted and processed as normal Ethernet, with the frame check sequence calculated and appended as part of data link layer transmission.
sections.eli5: To send, wrap the Ethernet message with a tiny header and send it as an IP package. To receive, check that it's really EtherIP, unwrap the Ethernet message, and pass it on.

sections.title: Security and Limitations
sections.content:
EtherIP can improve security by enabling the transfer of encrypted Ethernet payloads across untrusted networks. However, if a firewall permits EtherIP traffic to pass through, it may enable arbitrary communications that bypass the firewall's intended policy. Additional checking of frames may be necessary to ensure that security policies are not violated.

The biggest limitation of EtherIP is that it does not protect against infinite loops. When bridge-like stations forward Ethernet frames via EtherIP tunnels, frames can loop endlessly between multiple bridge-like stations, especially when broadcast or multicast destination addresses are used. The construction of a tree topology to prevent loops is left to the human configuring the bridge-like stations, which is error-prone. The IETF Pseudo Wire Emulation working group developed more sophisticated tunneling mechanisms that address these and other deficiencies of EtherIP.
sections.eli5: EtherIP can help hide information by letting encrypted messages travel across the internet. But the tiny protocol does not stop messages from going in circles forever if the network is set up wrong.
